• Resolver rules can be shared across accounts using AWS Resource Access Manager, enabling centralized DNS forwarding management.
  • Resolver endpoints must be deployed in at least two AZs for high availability, and each endpoint supports up to 10,000 queries per second per IP address.
  • Route 53 Resolver also supports DNS Firewall, which allows you to filter and block DNS queries to known malicious domains.

questions.title: Security Groups vs. NACLs
questions.scenario: A junior engineer is troubleshooting connectivity to an EC2 instance. The security group allows inbound SSH (port 22) from the office IP range, but SSH connections are timing out. Investigation reveals that the subnet's Network ACL has a deny rule for inbound port 22 that is evaluated before the allow rule.
questions.questionText: Why is the NACL deny rule blocking traffic even though the security group allows it?

choices.text: NACLs are evaluated before security groups, and NACL rules are processed in order — the deny rule has a lower rule number than the allow rule
The security group rule is not applied because the instance is in a public subnet
NACLs only apply to outbound traffic, not inbound
Security groups always take precedence over NACLs

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: NACLs are stateless and process rules in numerical order — the first matching rule (by rule number) determines whether traffic is allowed or denied.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Network ACLs are evaluated at the subnet level before traffic reaches the instance's security group. NACL rules are processed in order of rule number (lowest first). The first rule that matches the traffic determines the outcome — if a deny rule with a lower number matches before an allow rule, the traffic is denied and subsequent rules are not evaluated. Security groups, which are stateful and allow-only, are evaluated after the NACL. To fix this, the engineer should either remove the deny rule or renumber the allow rule to have a lower number than the deny rule.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Security groups are stateful (return traffic is automatically allowed), while NACLs are stateless (you must explicitly allow both inbound and outbound traffic, including ephemeral port ranges for return traffic).
  • The default NACL allows all inbound and outbound traffic. Custom NACLs deny all traffic by default (the implicit * deny rule).
  • Best practice is to use security groups as the primary firewall and NACLs as a coarse secondary layer — avoid complex NACL rule sets, as they are harder to manage and troubleshoot than security groups.

questions.title: PrivateLink for Service Exposure
questions.scenario: A SaaS provider runs their application in a VPC and wants to offer it to customers in different AWS accounts. Customers should be able to access the service using private IP addresses within their own VPCs, without requiring VPC peering, Transit Gateway, or internet access.
questions.questionText: Which AWS networking feature allows the SaaS provider to expose their service privately to customers in other accounts without requiring network-level connectivity between VPCs?

choices.text: VPC peering with cross-account authorization
AWS PrivateLink with a Network Load Balancer and VPC endpoint service
AWS App Mesh with cross-account service discovery
Route 53 private hosted zones shared across accounts

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: PrivateLink exposes a service behind an NLB as a VPC endpoint in the consumer's account — traffic flows over the AWS backbone with no VPC-to-VPC networking required.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: AWS PrivateLink creates a private connection between VPCs without VPC peering or Transit Gateway. The service provider places their application behind a Network Load Balancer (NLB) and creates a VPC endpoint service. Customers create an Interface VPC endpoint in their VPC, which provisions ENIs with private IP addresses. Traffic from the customer's VPC to the endpoint flows over the AWS network to the provider's NLB. There is no route table configuration, no CIDR overlap concerns, and the provider's VPC is not exposed to the customer — only the specific service endpoint.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• PrivateLink supports acceptance workflows — the provider can require manual approval before a consumer's endpoint connection is activated.
  • The consumer sees the service as a local ENI with a private IP, and can optionally enable private DNS names to access the service via a friendly hostname.
  • Many AWS services (over 100) are available via PrivateLink Interface endpoints, including S3 (Interface endpoint), SQS, SNS, and Secrets Manager.

questions.title: VPC Flow Logs Analysis
questions.scenario: The security team notices intermittent connectivity issues between two EC2 instances in different subnets within the same VPC. They need to determine whether traffic is being accepted or rejected at the network layer, and identify the specific source/destination IPs and ports involved.
questions.questionText: Which AWS feature captures network flow data including accepted and rejected traffic at the VPC, subnet, or ENI level?

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail data events
Amazon Inspector network assessments
VPC Flow Logs
AWS Network Firewall logs

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: VPC Flow Logs capture information about IP traffic going to and from network interfaces, including whether the traffic was accepted or rejected.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: VPC Flow Logs capture metadata about IP traffic flowing through network interfaces in your VPC. You can create flow logs at the VPC, subnet, or individual ENI level. Each flow log record includes the source/destination IP, source/destination port, protocol, number of packets, bytes transferred, and whether the traffic was ACCEPTED or REJECTED by security groups or NACLs. Flow logs can be published to CloudWatch Logs, S3, or Kinesis Data Firehose for analysis. They are essential for troubleshooting connectivity issues and security analysis.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Flow logs capture metadata only — not packet contents. For packet inspection, you need a Network Firewall, traffic mirroring, or a third-party tool.
  • Custom flow log formats allow you to include additional fields like TCP flags, flow direction, traffic path (through NAT, TGW, etc.), and the sublocation type.
  • Flow logs have a capture window of approximately 10-15 minutes — they are not real-time. For real-time traffic analysis, consider Traffic Mirroring or inline inspection.

questions.title: Cost Explorer and Savings Plans
questions.scenario: A finance team analyzes their AWS bill and finds that EC2 and Fargate compute costs account for 60% of their monthly spend. The workloads are steady-state — running 24/7 with predictable capacity. They want to reduce compute costs by committing to a usage level for 1 or 3 years.
questions.questionText: Which AWS purchasing option provides the most flexibility to save on compute costs across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda with a usage-based commitment?

choices.text: EC2 Reserved Instances with Standard 3-year term
On-Demand Capacity Reservations
Spot Instances with a Spot Fleet
Compute Savings Plans with a 1 or 3-year term

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Compute Savings Plans apply to EC2, Fargate, and Lambda across any Region, instance family, OS, or tenancy — they commit to a dollar-per-hour spend, not a specific instance type.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Compute Savings Plans offer up to 66% savings over On-Demand pricing by committing to a consistent amount of compute usage (measured in $/hour) for 1 or 3 years. Unlike Reserved Instances, which are locked to a specific instance family, Region, and OS, Compute Savings Plans apply across EC2 instance families, Regions, operating systems, tenancies, and also cover Fargate and Lambda usage. This flexibility means you can change instance types or even shift workloads between services without losing savings. EC2 Instance Savings Plans offer deeper discounts but are locked to an instance family and Region.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Savings Plans are applied automatically to your highest-cost usage first, maximizing savings without manual management.
  • Cost Explorer provides Savings Plans recommendations based on your historical usage patterns, showing estimated savings for different commitment levels.
  • Reserved Instances still offer slightly deeper discounts than Savings Plans for stable, predictable workloads locked to a specific instance type and Region — up to 72% for 3-year all-upfront Standard RIs.

questions.title: AWS Budgets Alerts
questions.scenario: A project manager wants to receive an email alert when the team's AWS spending reaches 80% of their $10,000 monthly budget. They also want a second alert at 100% to prevent unexpected overages.
questions.questionText: Which AWS service should the project manager use to set threshold-based spending alerts?

choices.text: AWS Cost Explorer with saved reports
Amazon CloudWatch billing alarms
AWS Budgets with alert thresholds and SNS notifications
AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: AWS Budgets allows you to set custom cost and usage budgets with configurable alert thresholds that notify via email or SNS.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: AWS Budgets lets you create cost, usage, and reservation budgets with configurable alert thresholds. You can set multiple alerts on a single budget — for example, at 80% and 100% of the $10,000 monthly budget. Notifications can be sent via email or SNS topics. Budgets also support forecasted cost alerts (alerting when projected end-of-month spending will exceed the budget) and can trigger automated actions like applying an SCP to restrict new resource creation. Cost Explorer provides analysis but not real-time threshold alerts.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• AWS Budgets supports up to 5 alert thresholds per budget, with separate notification lists for each threshold.
  • Budget Actions can automatically apply IAM policies, SCPs, or target running instances (stop/terminate) when a threshold is breached — enabling automated cost control.
  • Budgets can be scoped to specific services, linked accounts, tags, or cost categories, allowing granular team-level or project-level budgets.

questions.title: Right-Sizing EC2 Instances
questions.scenario: An operations team suspects their EC2 fleet is over-provisioned. CloudWatch metrics show that 60% of instances consistently use less than 20% CPU and less than 30% memory. They want data-driven recommendations for downsizing instances to reduce costs.
questions.questionText: Which AWS service provides right-sizing recommendations based on historical utilization data?

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor performance checks
Amazon Inspector resource assessments
AWS Cost Explorer right-sizing recommendations
AWS Systems Manager Inventory

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Cost Explorer analyzes your EC2 usage metrics and provides specific instance type recommendations (modify or terminate) based on utilization patterns.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: AWS Cost Explorer's right-sizing recommendations analyze 14 days of EC2 utilization data (CPU, memory via CloudWatch agent, network, disk) and suggest specific instance type changes or terminations for underutilized instances. Each recommendation shows the current cost, recommended instance type, estimated savings, and the utilization metrics that drove the recommendation. AWS Compute Optimizer provides similar but more detailed recommendations using machine learning. Trusted Advisor has basic underutilized EC2 checks but with less granular recommendations.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• AWS Compute Optimizer (an alternative) uses machine learning to analyze utilization patterns and can recommend across EC2, EBS, Lambda, and Auto Scaling groups — it provides more granular analysis than Cost Explorer.
  • Right-sizing should be done before purchasing Reserved Instances or Savings Plans, as committing to oversized instances locks in waste.
  • Memory utilization requires the CloudWatch agent — without it, recommendations are based solely on CPU, network, and disk, which may be insufficient for memory-intensive workloads.

questions.title: S3 Intelligent-Tiering
questions.scenario: A data analytics team stores petabytes of log data in S3. Access patterns are unpredictable — some datasets are queried daily for weeks, then not accessed for months, then suddenly accessed again. The team wants to minimize storage costs without managing lifecycle policies or risking retrieval delays when data is needed.
questions.questionText: Which S3 storage class automatically moves objects between access tiers based on actual access patterns with no retrieval fees?

choices.text: S3 Standard with lifecycle policies transitioning to S3 Glacier after 90 days
S3 Standard-IA with S3 Batch Operations for manual tier changes
S3 One Zone-IA with lifecycle transition to S3 Glacier Deep Archive
S3 Intelligent-Tiering

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between frequent, infrequent, archive instant, archive, and deep archive tiers — with no retrieval fees and no operational overhead.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: S3 Intelligent-Tiering monitors access patterns per object and automatically moves objects between tiers. Objects not accessed for 30 days move to Infrequent Access (40% savings), 90 days to Archive Instant Access (68% savings), and optionally to Archive (90 days) and Deep Archive (180 days) tiers. When accessed, objects are automatically moved back to the Frequent Access tier with no retrieval fees or latency penalty (for the Frequent, Infrequent, and Archive Instant tiers). There is a small monthly monitoring and automation fee per object. This is ideal for unpredictable access patterns where lifecycle policies cannot be tuned effectively.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• The Archive and Deep Archive tiers in Intelligent-Tiering are opt-in — you must enable them. Objects in these tiers have retrieval latency (minutes to hours) but still no retrieval fees beyond the standard request charges.
  • Intelligent-Tiering has a minimum object size of 128 KB for monitoring — smaller objects are always stored in the Frequent Access tier and not monitored.
  • The monitoring fee is $0.0025 per 1,000 objects per month. For buckets with many small, frequently accessed objects, this fee can offset savings — it is most cost-effective for larger objects with unpredictable access.

questions.title: Tagging for Cost Allocation
questions.scenario: A company runs multiple projects on a single AWS account. The finance team needs to break down the monthly AWS bill by project to charge each team for their usage. Resources are not currently identifiable by project in the billing reports.
questions.questionText: What should the operations team implement to enable per-project cost allocation in AWS billing reports?

choices.text: Create separate AWS accounts for each project
Enable detailed billing reports and manually parse them by resource ID
Apply cost allocation tags (e.g., Project=TeamA) to resources and activate them in the Billing console
Use AWS Cost Categories to manually assign costs

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Cost allocation tags are key-value pairs applied to AWS resources that appear as columns in Cost and Usage Reports, enabling filtering and grouping by project.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Cost allocation tags are metadata key-value pairs (e.g., Project=TeamA, Environment=Production) applied to AWS resources. After tagging resources, you activate the tag keys as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing console. Once activated, these tags appear as filterable columns in Cost Explorer and the Cost and Usage Report, enabling the finance team to group, filter, and allocate costs by project. Tags must be applied consistently to all resources — use Tag Policies (via AWS Organizations) and AWS Config rules to enforce tagging compliance.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• There are two types of cost allocation tags: user-defined (you create and apply them) and AWS-generated (e.g., aws:createdBy). Both must be activated in the Billing console to appear in reports.
  • Tags are not retroactive — they only appear in billing data from the month they are activated. Historical costs before tagging cannot be broken down by tag.
  • AWS Cost Categories provide a rule-based alternative — you define rules to categorize costs by account, service, tag, or other dimensions without requiring tags on every resource.

questions.title: Spot Instances with Capacity Management
questions.scenario: A machine learning team runs large batch training jobs that take 2-6 hours. They are cost-sensitive and want to use Spot Instances for up to 90% savings. However, Spot interruptions have caused jobs to restart from scratch, wasting time and money. They need a strategy to handle interruptions gracefully.
questions.questionText: Which approach minimizes the impact of Spot Instance interruptions on long-running batch workloads?

choices.text: Use only a single instance type to get the lowest Spot price
Use Spot Blocks (defined-duration Spot Instances) for guaranteed 6-hour capacity
Set a maximum Spot price equal to the On-Demand price to prevent interruptions
Use a diversified Spot Fleet across multiple instance types and AZs, with application-level checkpointing

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Diversifying across instance types and AZs reduces the chance of simultaneous Spot interruptions. Application checkpointing lets you resume from the last saved state rather than restarting from scratch.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: The best strategy combines infrastructure diversification with application resilience. A Spot Fleet (or EC2 Fleet) configured with the capacity-optimized allocation strategy selects from multiple instance types and AZs, choosing pools with the lowest interruption probability. Application-level checkpointing (saving training state to S3 or EFS periodically) means that if an instance is interrupted, a replacement can resume from the last checkpoint instead of restarting. Setting a high max price does not prevent interruptions — Spot instances are interrupted based on capacity, not price. Spot Blocks are discontinued.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• The capacity-optimized allocation strategy selects Spot pools with the most available capacity, reducing interruption frequency. This is generally better than the lowest-price strategy for workloads sensitive to interruptions.
  • EC2 provides a 2-minute interruption notice via instance metadata and CloudWatch Events, which the application can use to trigger a final checkpoint before termination.
  • For mixed workloads, EC2 Auto Scaling groups support a mixed instances policy with On-Demand base capacity and Spot for the remainder, ensuring minimum capacity even during Spot shortages.

questions.title: Data Transfer Cost Optimization
questions.scenario: A company's AWS bill shows that data transfer costs are the third largest line item. Most of the charges are from data transfer between AZs within the same Region, driven by a microservices architecture where services in different AZs communicate heavily over private IP addresses.
questions.questionText: Which architectural change would most effectively reduce inter-AZ data transfer costs while maintaining high availability?

choices.text: Implement zone-aware routing to prefer same-AZ communication while maintaining multi-AZ deployment for HA
Use VPC endpoints for all inter-service communication
Move all services to a single Availability Zone
Compress all data before sending it between services

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Cross-AZ data transfer is charged at $0.01/GB in each direction. Same-AZ traffic over private IPs is free. Zone-aware routing minimizes cross-AZ calls while keeping multi-AZ for resilience.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Data transfer between AZs costs $0.01/GB in each direction (total $0.02/GB round trip), while same-AZ traffic using private IPs is free. Zone-aware (AZ-affinity) routing configures services to prefer calling instances of downstream services in the same AZ. For example, ALB's availability zone affinity, EKS topology-aware routing, or App Mesh locality-based load balancing can keep most traffic within the same AZ. Services remain deployed across multiple AZs for high availability, but the majority of inter-service traffic stays within a single AZ. Moving to a single AZ (option A) eliminates HA and is not recommended.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Kubernetes topology-aware routing (topologyKeys or topology-aware hints) directs traffic to pods in the same AZ, significantly reducing cross-AZ charges in EKS clusters.
  • For services using SQS, consider AZ-aware message processing — consumers process messages from the same AZ where they were produced to reduce cross-AZ data transfer.
  • VPC Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) are free, but Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) incur data processing charges — they do not reduce inter-AZ transfer costs for service-to-service communication.
